metadata.title: ICT, learning environment and student characteristics as potential cross-country predictors of academic achievement

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2018 data aggregated to country-level mean test scores (reading, mathematics, science) for 41 countries/economies, rather than reporting a student-level microdata analysis with explicit complex-survey weighting. The methodology section describes stepwise multiple linear regression with robust standard errors to address heteroscedasticity, but it does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights. Because the analysis is conducted on aggregated mean scores and the paper does not specify weight variables (e.g., student/sampling weights), weighting cannot be confirmed from the text. Analysts using the underlying PISA microdata would typically apply PISA sampling weights when estimating population-representative relationships, but this paper’s reported workflow does not document such a procedure.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe any missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation) for the 30 explanatory variables and 3 dependent mean-score outcomes. Given that the analysis is restricted to 41 countries/economies where the needed variables are available, the effective missingness appears to be handled through country/variable availability rather than an explicit student-level imputation or deletion rule. This omission limits transparency about how missing questionnaire or index components were treated within the included countries.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study starts from OECD PISA 2018 and uses only the subset of countries/economies for which the required variables are available, resulting in 41 countries/economies (listed in the footnote). The dependent variables are country-level mean test scores for 15-year-old students in reading, mathematics, and science, and the explanatory variables are country-level averages/indices derived from PISA 2018 (for school, ICT, and student learning climate constructs) plus country-level political/economic indicators from external sources (World Bank and multiple 2018 indices). The paper does not report student-level inclusion/exclusion rules beyond the country/variable availability constraint, and it does not document an explicit missing-data handling method for incomplete questionnaire/index components.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Stepwise multiple linear regression with robust standard errors; R2=0.8989; Root MSE=0.0474; F(18,22)=14.10; Prob>F=0.0000. Significant predictors include leacs (-0.008***), ictihd (0.001***), qsmem (-0.003***), slcbs (0.12*), slcdc (0.218***), slcff (0.134*), slcse (0.225***), slcte (-0.387***), slcts (-0.128**), peeefi (-0.005**), peefiw (-0.001**), peegci (0.008***), peegdp (-0.002*).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading the study leveraged Average class size, Internet time at home (weekend), Inadequate educational material, Sense of belonging at school, and Disciplinary climate to predict Reading achievement (log of mean score), finding that smaller classes, more home internet time, and stronger belonging/discipline were associated with higher reading scores while inadequate educational material and higher teacher enthusiasm/support were associated with lower scores. This indicates that improving learning conditions (especially educational materials) and fostering supportive school climates may be more actionable for reading outcomes than simply increasing teacher enthusiasm, though the study’s correlational regression design and lack of documented PV/missing-data handling limit causal interpretation.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Stepwise multiple linear regression with robust standard errors; R2=0.9156; Root MSE=0.0427; F(13,27)=42.61; Prob>F=0.0000. Significant predictors include leacs (-0.007***), ictihd (0.001**), qsmem (-0.002***), slcbs (0.214***), slcdc (0.101***), slcff (0.142***), slcls (-0.065**), slcse (0.153**), slcte (-0.203***), slcts (-0.122***), peefiw (-0.002***), peegci (0.006***), peegdp (-0.002***).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics the study leveraged Average class size, Internet time at home (weekend), Inadequate educational material, Fear of failure, and Self-efficacy to predict Mathematics achievement (log of mean score), finding that smaller classes, more home internet time, and stronger student motivation/climate indicators were associated with higher mathematics scores while inadequate educational material and higher teacher enthusiasm/support were associated with lower scores. This indicates that mathematics gains may depend on both resource adequacy (materials) and student engagement-related school climate, but the results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects given the study’s regression framework and limited reporting on missing-data and PV procedures.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Stepwise multiple linear regression with robust standard errors; R2=0.9103; Root MSE=0.0469; F(20,20)=22.82; Prob>F=0.0000. Significant predictors include leacs (-0.008***), ictihd (0.002***), qsmem (-0.003***), less (0.112**), slcbs (0.142*), slcdc (0.298***), slcff (0.181*), slcse (0.153**), slcte (-0.366***), slcts (-0.158**), peefiw (-0.002***), peegci (0.005**), peegdp (-0.003***).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Science the study leveraged Average class size, Internet time at home (weekend), Inadequate educational material, Fear of failure, and Disciplinary climate to predict Science achievement (log of mean score), finding that better material adequacy and stronger student belonging/discipline/fear-of-failure climate were associated with higher science scores while inadequate educational material and higher teacher enthusiasm/support were associated with lower scores. This indicates that science improvement strategies should prioritize educational material quality and classroom climate supports, while also re-examining how teacher practices are measured and interpreted, though causality cannot be inferred from this correlational stepwise regression.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes OECD PISA 2018 data for 41 countries/economies, using country-level mean test scores for 15-year-olds in reading, mathematics, and science as dependent variables. The authors apply stepwise multiple linear regression (backward elimination/forward addition) with robust standard errors to address heteroscedasticity, and they report high model fit across subjects (R²≈0.90; Root MSE <0.05). Across the three models, the strongest and most consistent predictors include average class size (negative association), home internet time (positive), inadequate educational material (negative), and student school-climate variables such as belonging, disciplinary climate, and fear of failure (positive). Teacher enthusiasm and teacher support show negative associations with achievement in all subjects where significant. Limitations include the correlational nature of regression, lack of documented missing-data handling, and no explicit reporting of how PVs and country-level aggregation were handled for the mean-score outcomes.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper does not train or evaluate machine-learning algorithms; it uses stepwise multiple linear regression with robust standard errors. Therefore, the ML technique fields are intentionally left empty (no Random Forest/XGBoost/etc.), and the extraction focuses on the regression-based predictive modeling of achievement means. This is an empirical cross-country regression study rather than an ML-prediction pipeline, so no ML primary model can be assigned.
